posts.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups.
To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle.
We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t.
Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type.
That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. 
From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop
Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step.
With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it.
With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration.
When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t.
So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change.
With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible:

Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike.
Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers.
Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. 
Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action.  
The Operating Model
That ownership model needs machinery with five key components:
Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone.
Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke.
Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. 
Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review.
Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created.
Adapting the Environment to the Models
The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. 
Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. 
Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from.
Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. 
This gave us three things at once: 
Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. 
Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. 
No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. 
The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect.
Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing
Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause.
One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions.
While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness.
Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed
We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places:
Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself.
Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. 
What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it.

Did It Work?
Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile:


Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults.
Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality.
Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. 
The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework.
What Worked, and What Did Not
 
Acknowledgements 
We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions.

posts.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record!
There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. 
Some highlights:
WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second.
Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak.
Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. 
Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline.
Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6.
Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup.
Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball 
Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. 
But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament.

It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. 
Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern.
Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention
Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand.
Region-Specific Capacity
Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament.
Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges
For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience.
During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours.

Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final.
 Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament.
 Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality.
 Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems.
 Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after.
All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics.
WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes
Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption.
That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed.
Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t.
We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms.
We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. 
We Stay Ready Year-Round
Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one.
Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.

posts.title: Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta.
Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes.
Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality.
Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp. 
We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true.
As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start.

posts.title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva
When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.
This post is about that search for the needle.
The Four hours before a fix
Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?
As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.
The MELT Layer
“What caused the issue?”
Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.
MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.
The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:
What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out
The timeline of an investigation
So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?
A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours
In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.
The disagreement underneath
The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.
It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.
Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.
The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.
What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.
The Ontology
This agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.
api-gateway   rdf:type       ops:Application .
api-gateway   ops:ownedBy    "Team Bedrock" .
api-gateway   ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .
INC-5377      rdf:type       ops:Incident .
INC-5377      ops:affects    api-gateway .
INC-5377      ops:severity   "SEV 2" .
In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.
“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.
We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.
We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.
The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).
Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.
Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:

There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.
The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.
The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:

Creating determinism from non-determinism
Building this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.
The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:
# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:
category  IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"]
sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"]
# Result — a deterministic triple:
thread:123  slack:category          "incident" .
thread:123  slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .
There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:
The five layers to create determinism from non-determinism
Enrichers: Agents as entropy reducers
We use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:
class Enricher:
    async def _enrich_async(self, ...):
        raw    = await self.fetch(...)      # 1. read noisy input
        result = self.analyze(raw)          # 2. process (may be stochastic)
        graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X))   # 3. emit TYPED triples
        graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value)))
        return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)
Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:

every entity carries an rdf:type,
every URI follows a single naming scheme, and
the catalog gates every ops:Application.

Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.
This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.
The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chains
The correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.
The Correlation Engine
The role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.
A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.
The knowledge flywheel
Each harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.
The Knowledge Flywheel
Observe collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.

Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.
Putting the graph to work
On top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:

Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.
Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.
If you want to build one of these
A fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.

Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.
Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.
Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.
Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.
Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.
Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.
Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.
Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.

What comes next
The graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.
Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.
Acknowledgements
None of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.

Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

posts.title: Small Talk with Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What is Small Talk?
Small Talk is our short Q&A with founders from the JetBrains Startup Program. They answer a handful of questions in their own words about what they’re building, why they started, and what they’ve figured out along the way. No pitch, no polish – just a two-minute read to meet the person behind the product.
This time, we’re talking to Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia, a nutrition app that has grown to 10 million+ users in Latin America and beyond. He shares how his team brought four kinds of databases together in one place, why the rapid advancement of AI made JetBrains the first company his team went to for help, and how a small engineering team achieved a pace of one major feature per month.
Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia
Fitia is an AI-powered meal planning and calorie tracking app. Founded in Peru in 2019 by Piero Linares and Ulises Olave and backed by Y Combinator (Summer 2021), it’s the top nutrition app in Latin America and is now scaling in the US. Fitia joined the JetBrains Startup Program to help their lean team ship even faster by bringing DataGrip and GoLand into their workflow.
TL;DR
Fitia’s AI coach processes more than 30 million food logs a month, alongside data on weight, sleep, steps, and water. As the product has evolved, this data has been spread across different database types and providers.
DataGrip has given Fitia’s team one central place to work with all their databases, including PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Azure, and Redis. Its built-in AI features have also helped the team cut query times from hours down to mere seconds.
GoLand has helped Fitia roughly double their development speed on its Go microservices. They now ship three times faster than before, at a rate of one major feature per month.
What is Fitia, for someone who’s never used it?
Fitia is a meal-planning and calorie-tracking app. You tell it your goal – whether that’s losing weight or gaining muscle – and it builds a personalized plan that adapts to your data, your progress, and the foods you actually like to eat. The engine behind this is our own AI coach. We’re the top nutrition app in Latin America, and this year the goal is to become a leading health and fitness app in the US, too.
What was the biggest challenge you faced as Fitia grew?
Data. We store food records for all our users. This means more than 30 million items logged every month, plus data on weight, sleep, steps, and water intake. As our data grew, it ended up spread across several different database types and providers, and keeping integrity across all of them became a challenge. Even a simple query became a real headache in that kind of fragmented setup.
How did you deal with that?
We centralized everything in one place. We pulled our PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Azure, and Redis databases into DataGrip, so instead of jumping between providers, we could work with all our data in a single tool. And after centralizing it, we’ve been able to leverage DataGrip’s built-in AI as well. The query suggestions cut work that used to take hours down to seconds, especially against those complex multi-provider setups.
Why JetBrains?
We’d been using JetBrains tools from early on, so when AI started advancing at an almost absurd pace, JetBrains was the first company we turned to. Every month one of the big providers would release a better model, which meant we could suddenly deliver more features, and faster. We needed every developer to be fast enough to ship powerful features every month without expanding the team, and we needed one tool that covered the whole path, from writing the code to deploying it. We applied to the Startup Program, got accepted in a few days, and within a week the team was using DataGrip and GoLand daily.
Was there anything that surprised you?
How well integrated the AI is. At first, we were just focused on getting more efficient with solid IDEs. We didn’t expect the AI to be built in so natively. The context-aware chat lets you ask questions right inside the IDE, using your own code as context, and that changed how we worked more than we thought it would.
What specific impact has GoLand had?
With GoLand, we roughly doubled our development speed for our Go microservices. The code suggestions and optimization tooling let us build and deploy faster, which means our mobile team can rely on clean, reliable backend services and ship features much faster. The product goal is one major feature every month. That used to take us about three times as long. This year we’ve been holding that pace consistently.
Where does Fitia go from here?
AI has opened up possibilities in nutrition that were almost unimaginable before, from identifying food in a photo to reading a user’s data and giving personalized recommendations. Our strategy isn’t to compete with the big model providers – it’s to build on top of them, using their capabilities while training on our own community data, so we can create features that actually mean something to our users. Beyond that, we’ll just keep focusing on developer efficiency, because that’s what lets a small team move like a big one.




Read the full case study here.
JetBrains Startup Program FAQ
Q: Do I qualify?
A: You qualify if your company is privately owned, established within the last five years, and has a website or other discoverable online presence.
Q: Where do I apply?
A: You can apply here.
Q: What is the timeline for the JetBrains Startup Program application process?
A: After you apply, our team will review your application within 48 hours. If you meet the criteria, you will receive an acceptance email, followed by a quote for the products. If you’re not accepted, our team will get in touch and share our reasoning. An application may be unsuccessful either due to missing information (e.g., a document or website) or because you do not meet our eligibility requirements (e.g., your business is more than five years old).
Q: What products are included in the terms “IDE subscription” and “team or learning tool subscription”?
A: A variety of products are available through IDE subscriptions, including IDEs as well as .NET and Visual Studio tools. “Team tool subscription” refers to team tools, including TeamCity, YouTrack, Datalore, Qodana, and our learning tool (JetBrains Academy).

posts.title: Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users’ Task Flows
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Left: SWE-Bench Pro, where each task is a single user message, almost always a new feature or a bug fix. Right: the first five developer messages in sessions of software engineers working in JetBrains IDEs, counting only sessions with at least three messages. Each column is a message position, colored Cblocks are request types, and band widths show how often one type follows another.
This post summarizes our paper Opinion: Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users’ Task Flows, accepted to the Evaluation of Interactive Agents workshop at NeurIPS 2026.
At JetBrains Research, we recently analyzed 4,782 agent sessions of software engineers working in JetBrains IDEs and compared them with three public collections of agent conversations. In the developer sessions we looked at, fixing bugs and adding features account for less than half of what developers ask a coding agent to do. The rest contains questions about the codebase, planning, code review, refactoring, and command execution. In SWE-Bench Pro, on the other hand, 93.8% of tasks are features and bug fixes, and every task arrives as one complete message. That’s quite a difference.
That gap is the subject of this post. Our conclusion from the analysis is that there is no universal realistic coding-agent benchmark: a benchmark should be calibrated to measurements of a specific user population. SWE-TaskFlow is our contribution for doing this with any issue-derived benchmark; in this post, we apply it to SWE-Bench Pro.
What an issue-based benchmark measures
SWE-bench and its successors (SWE-Bench Pro, SWE-rebench, DeepSWE) build tasks from GitHub issues. The agent gets a repository checkout and the issue text, explores the code, edits it, and submits a patch. Tests decide whether the patch resolves the issue; the share of resolved issues is the resolve rate.
The infrastructure behind these tasks is expensive to build: i.e. a repository at the right commit, an environment where the code runs, and tests that verify the change. The interaction layer on top of it is fixed, however. The full specification arrives in one polished message, and one final patch is scored. 
Despite the fixed nature of the interaction layer, developers in an IDE work like that only some of the time. That is, half of the sessions we saw are a single message. In the rest, requirements come in pieces: Between one change request and the next, the developer asks the agent to explain how some part of the project works, to plan the next change, or to review what was done, while the earlier requirements still have to be carried along.
How developers actually use the agent
Each of the 4,782 sessions, which we call Production Sessions, is one conversation between a developer and the coding agent inside the IDE; together, they contain about 14,000 developer messages. We looked only at the developer’s side, and the figure below shows the distribution of messages across the Production Sessions.




The 4,782 sessions by number of developer messages (the chart calls them prompts). One developer message can trigger many agent actions.
Half of the sessions (50.9%) are a single message; about 15% run past five. Since our subject is interactive agents, the rest of the analysis is on the 33% of sessions with at least three developer messages, the long sessions, as follows.
An open-weight LLM (Gemma 4-31B) labeled every message with one of 16 request types, or intents: bug fix, new feature, explain, planning, code review, execute, and so on (all 16 are defined in the paper). The same classifier, with the same prompt, labeled the public collections and the SWE-Bench Pro issues, so every distribution in this post is measured on the same footing.
Across all sessions, bug fixes make up 26% of the labeled messages and new features 19%. In the long sessions, explanations of the project’s own code account for 6% of messages, and general programming questions for another 10%; planning, code review, refactoring, debugging, and execution make up most of the rest. SWE-Bench Pro, labeled the same way, comprises 55% new features, 39% bug fixes, 6% refactoring, and nothing else.
Session length and intent mix are two of the three components of a Task Flow; the third is the order in which intents follow one another. A session that opens with a feature request often continues with a question about existing behavior, a planning step, and a review request. 
How public collections compare
Our Production Sessions are for one user population. To see how much the picture depends on the population, we ran the classifier on 1,000 sessions from each of the public collections below and kept the long ones. Below, we include Sankey diagrams for each. The Sankey diagrams in this post are Task Flows, where each column is a message position, and the bands between columns are these transitions.
SpecStory consists of public IDE session exports, the data analyzed in Programming by Chat. 521 of its 1,000 sessions are long. Of the three, it sits closest to our sessions, with a larger share of planning.




DataClaw collects coding-agent sessions shared by the community. 585 of 1,000 are long. It is dominated by execution requests and short operational messages.




SWE-chat is a collection of coding-agent conversations from real users, gathered in a chat setting. 698 of 1,000 are long. Execution and planning are its largest intents.




These three corpora come from different products, different users, and different collection methods, so we do not compare them quantitatively. Still, a benchmark calibrated to any one of them would have a different mix of tasks and transitions than one calibrated to another. None of them is ground truth, and neither are our Production Sessions; the target has to be chosen and stated.
For our pilot, the target is the long Production Sessions. Calibrating to frequencies has a side effect: anything rare in the target gets pushed toward zero. Rare but consequential behaviors, such as a destructive shell command or a security-relevant review, should instead be evaluated in separate stress-test slices with their own task counts.
How SWE-TaskFlow adapts existing tasks
Building a new interactive benchmark for every target would throw away what issue-based benchmarks already have. Instead, we propose SWE-TaskFlow, which transforms an existing benchmark: it keeps the repository, the environment, the tests, and the original requirements, while regenerating only the user messages.
Splitting the issue into several requests
An LLM rewrites each issue as three ordered requests; we call them issue requests, since everything in them comes from the original issue. The agent works on the first before it sees the second. The split has to preserve every original requirement and add none; identifiers and code snippets are kept verbatim; each request has to be actionable in the repository state that the previous one left behind. A second model pass checks the result for completeness. 31 of the 731 public SWE-Bench Pro issues did not pass these splitting and evaluation checks and were left out, leaving 700 tasks.
Here is what it looks like for a qutebrowser issue titled “LinkedIn Fails Due to Missing Array.prototype.at Support in Older QtWebEngine”. The original issue is one message of about 1,000 characters. Split, it becomes:
Please fix the LinkedIn compatibility problem in qutebrowser on macOS with QtWebEngine 5.15.2. LinkedIn’s frontend JavaScript uses Array.prototype.at, which is missing from that older engine, so JavaScript execution fails and LinkedIn pages remain stuck or unresponsive. Add the qutebrowser JavaScript compatibility support needed so LinkedIn can load and function normally, using a polyfill to resolve the issue transparently.
The compatibility support should provide Array.prototype.at on QtWebEngine versions prior to 6.3 when it is not available natively, and it must be active and functional on LinkedIn domain pages and qutebrowser test domains. For array instances, positive integer indices should return the element at the specified index, while negative indices count backward from the end, with -1 referring to the last element.
Complete the behavior so indices outside the array bounds return undefined for both positive and negative indices. The polyfill must only be injected when the native Array.prototype.at method is not already available in the JavaScript environment.
The first request is enough to start working; the edge cases arrive later.
Adding questions about the repository
Explanations of the project’s own code are common in Production Sessions and absent from issue benchmarks, so we generate them. A model reads the repository together with the trajectory of an agent that previously solved the issue and proposes one to three questions. Each question must be answerable from the repository alone, stay valid both before and after the fix, and not give away the solution.
Every question ships with a reference answer and an executable proof script that collects evidence for the answer from the repository. At dataset creation, we run the script in a clean checkout and keep the question only if it passes, produces the evidence, and leaves the repository unchanged. This rules out, by construction, questions whose answers are not observable in the code (“why was it designed this way?”). At evaluation time, the agent answers in text, and a separate LLM judges the answer against the hidden reference and its evidence.
In the released configuration, the qutebrowser task above gets one question, placed between the first and second issue requests:
Concise answer: Trace how a relevant stylesheet configuration change updates both future QtWebEngine documents and the already loaded document, including CSS assembly, script replacement, execution world, subframe behavior, and the no-op path for unrelated options.
The reference answer names the two config options that trigger this path and walks through five files. The proof script performs a stylesheet config change against the real code, checks the resulting script registration and the call into the live page, and confirms that an unrelated option does nothing. The question is unrelated to Array.prototype.at: it comes from code the solving agent read along the way, not from the fix itself.
Picking sequences that match the target
Questions can go before, between, or after the issue requests, so each task has several candidate sequences. We pick one per task so that the benchmark as a whole resembles the long Production Sessions, as measured by the TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS). TFAS compares the three distributions (session lengths, intents, transitions) between target and benchmark with the Jensen-Shannon divergence and combines them into a 0–100 score. Pure splitting scores 59.6 against our target. Adding questions at fixed positions raises it to 75.6–77.1; letting an optimizer choose how many questions each task keeps and where they are placed raises it to 77.8. The result is 454 questions across 255 of the 700 tasks (113 tasks with one question, 85 with two, 57 with three), with 67 tasks carrying their questions only before the issue requests, 86 only after, and 102 interleaved. The other 445 tasks keep their three issue requests.




Task Flow of SWE-Bench Pro (left) and of the TFAS-optimized selection with TFAS 77.8 (right). One user prompt per issue becomes up to six sequential prompts of different types. Repositories, requested changes, and the final tests are unchanged.
In the right panel, the issue requests carry the task types that were already in the issues: bug fix, new feature, and some refactoring, the same three that make up all of SWE-Bench Pro on the left. Smaller intents also surface once an issue is split: debug, transformation, tests, planning, and a few others. These are not additions but parts of the original issue that the classifier folded into the dominant intent when it saw the issue as one message (a bug-fix issue that also asks for a regression test, for example) and that became visible as separate messages after the split. The only intent that comes from outside the issue is explain, carried by the repository questions.
Pilot results: four models, three setups
To evaluate SWE-TaskFlow, we ran GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.4 Mini, and Gemini 3.7 Flash through mini-swe-agent on the same 700 tasks, three runs per setup:
Single: The original issue in one message.
Split: The three requests, delivered one after another in a single conversation.
Split+QA: The TFAS-selected sequences with repository questions.




Means of three runs; whiskers are observed min–max. Colors are models, shapes are setups.
Splitting the issue into three messages made every model 2.0–2.6× more expensive per task. Since the repository, the tests, and the requirements did not change, the extra cost measures how much more effort an agent spends when the requirements arrive in pieces. Resolve rates moved less: GPT-5.6 Terra stayed flat, the other three dropped by 4–5 points on average, which is comparable to the spread between individual runs of the same setup. With three runs per setup, these results do not rank the models; they show that progressive disclosure reliably changes the effort and only weakly changes the outcome.
The LLM rewrite itself, rather than the sequencing, could also have made the tasks harder. A control condition, Concat, delivers the same three rewritten parts pasted into one message. For the three GPT models, with one run each, it lands next to Single on both cost and resolve rate, so the extra cost of Split comes from the sequential delivery, not from the rewording.
Adding the repository questions costs another 4%–24% on top of Split, depending on the model. On the 255 tasks that carry questions, the share of answers the judge marks correct (answer accuracy) ranges from 69.8% (GPT-5.4 Mini) to 83.0% (GPT-5.6 Terra).




Filled circles: answer accuracy. Hollow circles: resolve rate on the same 255 tasks, which is why these resolve values differ from the plot above.
A split trajectory also admits intermediate verification. After each issue request, we can snapshot the repository and rerun the tests, scoring only against the requirements revealed so far. In a 64-task ablation, both the resolve rate and test-pass rate grow with each issue turn, and the position of the questions does not move the curves. One task yields several verified checkpoints instead of a single final score. That is useful for diagnosis and potentially for training; we have not tried the latter.
What SWE-TaskFlow does not yet cover
SWE-TaskFlow currently generates two kinds of messages: issue requests and repository questions. Everything else in the Task Flow of real sessions (general programming questions, planning, code review, refactoring beyond what the issues already contain, execution, debugging without a fix) still needs its own generator and its own verifier, and for most of these, it is unclear how to check the response automatically. The measured Task Flow at least tells us which augmentations are missing and in what proportion. 
All messages are also fixed before the run. That gives exact replayability and paired comparisons, and it measures progressive disclosure, memory, and adaptation, but not how the agent handles feedback: the “user” cannot react to what the agent did. Reactive benchmarks with simulated users cover that at the price of trajectory variance; a full evaluation suite would combine a calibrated static core with targeted reactive slices. Beyond that, the classifier has no human-labeled accuracy set; some issues cannot be split, question difficulty depends on the model that writes them, and the pilot has three runs per setup.
Try it yourself
                                                    
The SWE-TaskFlow-SWE-Bench-Pro dataset on Hugging Face has 12 configurations as separate splits: the original prompts, the split prompts, the Split+QA variants, and QA-only sessions. Every question comes with its reference answer and proof script. Repositories, gold patches, and tests stay with the original SWE-Bench Pro release.

posts.title: Why We Still Need an IDE
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
I’ve been mulling this over for about a year now. The developer landscape has shifted to the point where you can’t scroll past the news without seeing someone declare “I never open my IDE anymore” or “I do everything in the terminal.” And those workflows genuinely work for some people. But not for everyone. I honestly believe IDEs embody why we love what we do. The question then becomes: how do we move forward as the world changes?
The workflow has changed. The environment needs to match it.
Coding agents are no longer an experiment; for many of us, they’re already an everyday part of building software. We aren’t just tab-completing anymore. We’re handing agents substantive tasks that touch multiple files, explore dependencies, and refactor across packages. The day-to-day rhythm of engineering is evolving: it’s less about typing line by line and more about steering intent.
JetBrains Rider looks more like a cockpit for agentic development these days: agent sessions, their status, and the full project context in one view.



Think of this shift like the move from hand-flying to using a modern aircraft’s flight computer. The computer can handle complex execution, but it is capable because it is connected to the plane’s instruments: navigation, altitude, speed, and engine data. The pilot doesn’t need to move every control at every moment, but still needs a cockpit where they can see the whole flight, understand what is happening, and intervene when the route changes.
Agentic software development works the same way. An agent can plan and carry out a substantial change, but it needs a rich environment around it, and so does the engineer directing it. Code analysis, navigation, dependency information, type checking, tests, and access to the systems around the code provide the context that a terminal or isolated session may not expose clearly. An agent may run a compiler or test; the IDE makes the result part of a connected picture of the project, so you can understand not just whether something failed, but what it affects and why.
The pilot also owns the flight, even when the computer is doing much of the work. The engineer owns what ships, even when the agent wrote most of the code. That means reviewing the change in context, understanding its consequences, and being able to explain and defend the result later.
And then there is judgment: deciding whether the proposed route is the right one, not merely whether the plane can reach its destination. An agent can produce a working implementation; the engineer still decides whether it fits the architecture, the users, and the problem worth solving.
This is where the role of the IDE becomes particularly interesting. It is the cockpit where agents and developers can see the same project, use the same instruments, and work together on the decisions that determine what gets shipped. A prompt can start the work. An IDE is where you steer, verify, and take responsibility for the result.
From “typing syntax” to “directing intent” 
This is the context problem. An agent can reason across your codebase, but if you can’t see what it’s seeing, you’re not actually steering it – you’re just hoping it got it right.
Agentic tools aren’t a passing fad. They’re a core part of how a lot of us build now, and that’s not going away. Being a good developer was never really about how fast you could type. Typing was just the mechanical part. The actual work was figuring out what required a change and deciding what to do about it. Typing took up so much of the day that it was easy to confuse it with the job itself.
Now that typing isn’t the bottleneck, the day looks different. You’re reading the agent’s plan before it runs. You’re catching the one edge case it missed. You’re asking whether the change it proposed is actually the right change, not just a working one. Less time producing code, more time deciding that the code is correct.
I built something recently in a stack I had basically no real experience with. I wanted to build a browser extension, but after reading the docs, I wasn’t clear how bootstrapping and configuring the project were done. 
Instead of learning every detail before I could begin, I pointed an agent at the problem. It handled much of the mechanical work, from creating the project to configuring it and getting the first pieces in place, all while I focused on what I wanted to build. I didn’t have to know the exact syntax or setup process to express the intent. The agent didn’t replace the learning. It gave me a working project I could explore, question, and improve instead of a blank file or empty workspace. Once I opened the IDE, I could see how the pieces fit together, trace unfamiliar code, and steer the next step from something real.
A few years ago, that project didn’t happen, or it happened much more slowly, because the barrier was always “I don’t know this well enough to get moving”. The agent lowered that barrier. It took care of some of the mechanical work so I could concentrate on the problem, the direction, and the decisions that mattered. 
It also pulls you into the bigger picture, even on small tasks. If an agent touches a dozen files for something that used to be a two-line fix, you’re the one who has to know whether that was the right dozen files. That means more of your day lives at the architectural level than it used to, with more thinking about how services depend on each other, what a change actually impacts downstream, and whether the agent’s plan fits how the system is supposed to work. A ticket/issue used to mean “I need to edit this function to solve this”. Now it means “I need to define the right shape of the entire change, then point the agent at the right things to edit”. That’s hard to do from a chat window. You’re watching an agent make real decisions about your codebase through an interface that shows you one message at a time. If these tools can reason across your whole project, you need to be able to see it across your whole project too, and how they are affecting it; otherwise, you’re just clicking approve. 
This is also where the IDE’s own tooling comes in, not just for you, but for the agent.
Verification and understanding are where ownership lives
This is the ownership problem. Code being correct and code being yours are two different things, and only one of them survives the postmortem.
Generating more code is easy now. An agent can write you a working function in seconds, and in a lot of cases, it will be fine on the first try. That’s not really the hard part anymore, and treating it like the hard part is how you end up shipping things nobody on your team actually understands.
The bottleneck moved to verification. Questions like: “Is this correct?”, “Does it handle the case your users actually hit?”, and “Does it match how the rest of the system is supposed to behave, not just how this one function behaves in isolation?” are what we worry about now. An agent can generate the code faster than you can read it, which means reading it, really reading it, not skimming diffs, is now the slow part of the job. That’s fine, because that was always supposed to be the slow part.
This matters because you can’t own code you don’t understand. If a bug shows up in something an agent wrote and your merge commit says “the agent wrote it”, good luck on that triage call or postmortem. Your name is on the commit, so you need to understand the change well enough to defend, debug, and explain it to someone else. That is what makes it actually yours, and that doesn’t happen by reading a chat summary of what the agent did. It happens by sitting with the actual change, in context, long enough to be sure. The agent isn’t the one who gets paged at 2:00 am, isn’t the one in the postmortem, and isn’t the one whose name is on the performance review. You are. Accountability doesn’t transfer just because the authorship did, and no team is going to accept “the agent did it” as a substitute for “I understood what I shipped”. 
This is also just what IDEs were already built for. Long before agents existed, the IDE’s main function was to let you verify the solution to a problem, allow you to jump to a definition, see where a function is called, catch a type error before it ships, and trace a variable back to where it came from. None of that functionality needs to be reinvented for agentic work; it just needs to be pointed at agent output instead of your own. The tool for understanding code has existed the entire time. The only new part is that you’re not only using your own code?  
Take pride in what you build
This is a judgment problem, and it was never really about agents at all.
This isn’t really a conversation about tools. It’s a conversation about what the discipline of software engineering is actually built on, and whether that survives the shift to agentic work or gets lost in it.
It’s easy to think, “I am typing almost none of the code myself,” and see it as being removed from the process. It isn’t, as long as the thinking behind it is still yours in every way that matters. You can type nothing and still be the one who devised the architecture, the one who knew why a particular approach was right, when the rest of your team thought otherwise, or the one who caught the thing the agent got subtly wrong before it shipped. That’s not a smaller job than writing every line by hand. It’s the same job it always was, with the typing taken out. 
The thing worth remembering is that engineers were never actually in the business of producing code. Engineers solve problems. Code was always just the medium that happened to require a lot of manual labor to produce, so the labor got mistaken for the craft. An agent that writes code faster than you can type isn’t replacing the craft; it’s removing the part of the job that was never really the point.
So take pride in the thing that was always the actual work: the judgment, the architecture, the final decision over what should exist and why. If an agent helps you get there faster, that’s not a smaller version of engineering. It’s the same standard, held just as seriously, moving at the speed the tools finally allow.
Every captain flying on autopilot still needs a cockpit to control the flight path. The instruments don’t replace the pilot; they’re what make the pilot capable of flying such a complicated machine safely. Think of the IDE as your coding cockpit. It’s not a “nice-to-have” around the agent. It’s the thing that makes directing one, instead of just talking to one, actually possible.
IDE tools for developers AND agents
IDEs are uniquely equipped to answer the problems stated above, just like the flight computer. We should look to give agents access to the same instruments and controls that the pilot has, as well as tools for validation and review. A rich IDE also gives you the opportunity to exercise your judgment, helping you understand and own the code, by providing everything you need to do the job.
LLMs are probabilistic. They’re guessing, well-informed guessing, but guessing nonetheless. Software engineering isn’t. A type system doesn’t have an opinion about whether the code compiles; it either does or doesn’t. That gap between how the agent thinks and how the system actually behaves is where most of the real bugs live. 
Right now, most of that gap gets closed after the fact. Some agents already run compilers, linters, and tests mid-task, which is genuinely useful because it catches errors that would have otherwise been shipped. But running a check and actually seeing the system the way a developer does aren’t the same thing. The agent gets a compiler or runtime error, possibly a stack trace. A human using an IDE gets the type checker, the linter, and the test suite integrated into actual navigation and context, not just a pass/fail, but the reason why. From there, you can trace its source and understand how it connects to the larger picture. The tooling isn’t missing from the agent’s loop anymore. What is missing is the depth that it is connected to, and the ability to select the right tool at the right time. 
The fix isn’t to make the agent better at guessing. It’s to help it make a more informed decision. The same deterministic intelligence the IDE gives you, like type resolution, linting, and real-time error checking, needs to be available to the agent while it is working, not just to the human reviewing it afterward. An agent that can check its own types mid-task, see a lint error the moment it writes that line, and run the test it just broke before it moves on, isn’t operating on the probability anymore. It’s operating with the same grounded truth your tools always have.
That’s the shift that is taking place. Not smarter agents, but the same deterministic tools we built for developers, finally pointed at the thing writing the code, instead of only at the person checking it afterward. 
Once agents can work with the same tools developers rely on, the next question is: who gets to choose those agents and tools? Developers should be able to use the best tool for the task without rebuilding their workflow or navigating a maze of configuration. The IDE should be the stable layer, connecting agents to rich development tools, but it is only useful if developers aren’t locked into one provider’s version of that workflow.
We can’t have AI walled gardens
Betting your entire workflow on one model provider is a real risk, not a hypothetical one. Providers can change pricing, get acquired, deprecate models, have outages, and end up falling behind the field for a few months. If switching providers requires changing your tools, workflows and configuration, then the cost of switching becomes a reason to stay, even when a better option is available. The goal isn’t to make developers manage a complicated collection of integrations. It’s the opposite: give them one dependable environment where they can use the agents and models THEY WANT, with the project context and development tools they need, without unnecessary friction.
This is where the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) can help. ACP gives IDEs and coding agents a shared way to communicate, reducing the need for a separate, custom integration every time a new agent is added.  That can make an agent feel native to the IDE without making the IDE dependent on a single provider. ACP takes away repetitive integration work; it doesn’t have to take away the developer’s choice. 
With Air, you can seamlessly add the agents you already use to your IDE with little effort, allowing you to use the tools you love without extra overhead.



This doesn’t even consider the fact that with every new model that comes out, the overall messaging is that it should be the primary model going forward. If your whole development pipeline is wired to a single provider’s API, every one of those events becomes your problem too. That’s not a tooling decision; it’s a dependency you’ve taken on without really deciding to. And we all know what happens when we take a dependency, it will eventually give us a headache when a change occurs. 
The fix isn’t picking the right provider. There isn’t a right one; whoever’s best today won’t necessarily be best in a month, and at the pace this field is moving, locking in early is how you end up stuck defending the choice you made for reasons that stopped being true. And when that new model eventually comes out, it has to go through the gauntlet of your software development needs before you feel comfortable “trusting” it. 
That means the IDE itself cannot be opinionated about which model is doing the work. Switching providers, running different models for different tasks, trying a new one the week it ships, none of that should require reconfiguring your whole setup. If changing models is a project, you won’t do it, and you’ll end up stuck with whatever you picked first by default rather than by choice. 
That’s really what Bring Your Own Keys (BYOK) comes down to in practice. You bring the credentials for the models and providers you choose, which is typically an API key or sometimes an account or subscription, and connect them to the IDE. The IDE remains the place where project context, code intelligence, tools, and review live. The provider supplies the model, while you retain control over usage, limits, and cost. Switching means selecting another configured provider or model, not rebuilding your workflow.
ACP and BYOK address different parts of the same problem. ACP helps an IDE connect to different agents through a common interface. BYOK lets developers choose the provider credentials behind that experience. One provides interoperability; the other preserves control. A native agent experience should make choice easier, not remove it. 
It’s not a nice-to-have for people who want to tinker with settings. It’s a way to keep the leverage on your side instead of the providers. You use what’s actually good right now, you drop what isn’t, and you’re never negotiating from a position where switching costs more than staying put.
Use the tools that solve the problem
The question we really have facing us is: Why not use agents and IDEs together? It is how. The goal of the software engineering discipline is to ultimately solve problems of the business using software. Over the years, the “software” has changed quite a bit, from walking up hills both ways in the snow to compile your punch cards to now just typing what you want and manifesting it into existence. I use agents in my IDE today, and the combination of the intelligence that the IDE provides with the reasoning and speed of an agent is a delightful experience. But this truly is the first step in transforming how we use these new sets of tools to do what we always did: solve a problem. 
That’s our take on where IDEs and agents are headed. We’re curious to hear yours.
